title: Memory: registers, RAM and the clock
task: Write `class Register` with `set(value, load)`, `tick()` and `out()`: the stored value changes only on `tick()`, and only when load is 1. Then write `class RAM(size)` from a list of Registers, with `set(addr, value, load)`, `tick()` and `read(addr)`. An address outside `0..size-1` raises `IndexError`.
hints: Re-read "Your interface": `set` only records the inputs, and `tick` is the only place a stored value changes. For RAM, re-read the paragraph about its one set of input wires.

`Register` remembers three things: its stored value and its two inputs. `tick` copies the input value into the stored value, but only if load is 1. `RAM` keeps a list of Registers: `set` makes sure only the newest address has load on, `tick` ticks them all, and `read` checks the address before reading.

`Register.__init__`: `self.value = 0`, `self.next_value = 0`, `self.load = 0`. `set` stores the inputs; `tick` does `if self.load: self.value = self.next_value`. `RAM`: `self.regs = [Register() for _ in range(size)]`. `set`: check the address, clear load on every register (`r.set(r.out(), 0)`), then `self.regs[addr].set(value, load)`. `read`: check the address, then `self.regs[addr].out()`.

quiz.q: A register holds 6. You call `set(9, 1)`, then `out()`, without ticking. What comes back?
quiz.why: `out()` gives the value from the last tick. The 9 is only waiting on the input wires until the next `tick()`.
RAM has one set of input wires, so the second `set` replaced the first. Only address 0 was written; address 3 still holds 0.

review.q: A register holds 3. You call `set(8, 0)`, `tick()`, then `out()`. What comes back?
review.why: Load was 0, so the tick kept the old value.

review.q: A register holds 0. You call `set(8, 1)`, `tick()`, `set(4, 0)`, `tick()`, then `out()`. What comes back?
review.why: The first tick stored 8. The second set has load 0, so the second tick keeps 8.

review.q: Logic whose output depends only on its inputs right now, with no memory, is called what?
review.why: Combinational logic (gates, adders, muxes) has no state. Sequential logic (registers, RAM) remembers, and changes on the clock.
